newsitem.title: HAITI: Grammy award-winning Haitian group draws big crowd.
newsitem.headline: Grammy award-winning Haitian group draws big crowd.

text.p: Thousands of Haitians took a break from their impoverished lives this weekend to hear the Grammy-winning Haitian-American rap group the Fugees perform a message of cultural pride and respect.
"We are going to show the world just what Haiti can offer," the group's lead singer Wyclef Jean told the crowd estimated at 70,000 on Saturday night.

People filled the Port-au-Prince waterfront for the six-hour outdoor concert, which showcased Haitian musicians performing on stage with the Haitian-American trio that has become one of the world's most popular music groups.
Their album "The Score" has sold 14 million copies internationally, and the group has won an array of international music awards, including a Grammy award for Best Rap Album in February.

It also won a Grammy for Best R&B Duo or Group Performance for the song "Killing Me Softly With His Song," as band members displayed the Haitian flag during a performance on the awards show, seen by a television audience estimated at 1.5 billion people in 170 countries.

The Fugees, and their advocacy of their homeland, are a rare success story for this poor and politically troubled country. Fugee mania has gripped Haiti since their homecoming from the United States for the benefit concert, whose proceeds were to benefit Haitian refugees repatriated from the neighbouring Dominican Republic.

Jean and another member, Praz, were born in Haiti and moved to the United States as children. The third member, Lauryn Hill, was born in the United States to Haitian parents. The group was honoured at the Presidential Palace on Friday and their music has played steadily on local radio.

"The Fugees reached the top of the music industry in the United States and have come back home to open the door for the rest of Haitian culture who, as a country deep in poverty, normally wouldn't have this chance," said Henry Robert Lourou, a Haitian musician who performed on stage with the group.
"This is the chance for people to see that Haiti is a civilised country," Wyclef said to the crowd, during an evening with no reports of major incidents of violence.

Among others who performed at the concert were Steve Marley, son of the Jamaican reggae legend Bob Marley; the Dominican artist Janna, and Manno Charlegmane, the mayor of Port-au-Prince and a popular folk singer who had given the group the key to the city on Thursday.
The concert ended with fireworks, rarely seen in the impoverished nation, the hemisphere's poorest, bringing wild cheers from the happy crowd.
